title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Remounting his horse, Prince Andrew lingered by the battery, watching the puff of smoke from the gun that had fired the shot. His eyes swept rapidly across the broad field, and he could see that the previously motionless French masses had begun to stir, and that there really was a battery on their left. The smoke from it hadn't yet cleared before another puff appeared, followed by the boom of a cannon. The battle had begun. Prince Andrew wheeled his horse around and galloped back to Grunth to find Prince Bagration. Behind him, the cannonade was growing louder and more frequent. Clearly, the Russian guns had started firing back. From the low ground where the parley had taken place that morning came the crackle of musket fire.

Lemarrois had just arrived at a gallop bearing Bonaparte's harsh letter, and Murat, humiliated and desperate to make up for his blunder, had immediately sent his forces forward to attack the center and outflank both Russian wings, hoping to crush this pitiful detachment before evening, before the Emperor himself could arrive.
"It's started. Here it is!" thought Prince Andrew, feeling the blood rush to his heart. "But where—and how—will I find my Toulon?"

Riding past the companies that had been eating porridge and drinking vodka just fifteen minutes ago, he saw the same scene everywhere: soldiers rapidly forming ranks, readying their muskets, and on every face the same fierce eagerness that burned in his own heart. "It's started! Here it is—terrifying but thrilling!" That was what each soldier's and each officer's face seemed to say.

Before he reached the earthworks being thrown up, he saw, in the dull light of the autumn evening, mounted men riding toward him. The one in front, wearing a Cossack cloak and a lambskin cap on a white horse, was Prince Bagration. Prince Andrew pulled up and waited; Bagration reined in his horse, recognized Prince Andrew, and gave him a nod. He kept looking straight ahead while Prince Andrew reported what he had observed.

The feeling—"It's started! Here it is!"—was visible even on Prince Bagration's hard, dark face with its half-shut, sleepy eyes. Prince Andrew studied that impassive face with anxious curiosity, wanting to know what, if anything, this man was thinking and feeling at that moment. "Is there actually anything behind that expressionless mask?" Prince Andrew wondered. Bagration inclined his head to signal agreement with what Prince Andrew told him and said, "Very good," in a tone suggesting that everything happening was exactly what he'd expected. Prince Andrew, out of breath from his hard ride, spoke quickly. Bagration, pronouncing his words with an Eastern accent, spoke especially slowly, as though to demonstrate that there was no need for haste. Still, he set his horse to a trot toward Tushin's battery. Prince Andrew followed with the rest of the staff. Behind Bagration rode a staff officer, the prince's personal adjutant, Zherkov, an orderly officer, the duty staff officer on a handsome bob-tailed horse, and a civilian—an accountant who had asked permission to observe the battle out of curiosity. The accountant, a stout man with a round face, looked around with a naive smile of delight and cut a strange figure among the hussars, Cossacks, and adjutants, bouncing along in his wool coat on a horse fitted with a convoy officer's saddle.
"He wants to see a battle," Zherkov said to Bolkonsky, nodding toward the accountant. "But he's already got a stomachache."
"Oh, stop it!" said the accountant with a beaming but slightly sly smile, flattered to be the butt of Zherkov's joke and deliberately playing up his own foolishness.
"It is very strange, mon Monsieur Prince," said the staff officer. (He remembered there was some special way to address a prince in French, but couldn't quite get it right.)
By now they were all approaching Tushin's battery, and a cannonball struck the ground in front of them.
"What was that that fell?" asked the accountant with a guileless smile.
"A French pancake," Zherkov replied.
"So that's what they fire at you? How frightening!" said the accountant.

He seemed to swell with satisfaction. He'd barely finished speaking when they heard another unexpectedly violent whistling that suddenly ended with a thud into something soft—f-f-flop!—and a Cossack riding slightly to the right and behind the accountant crashed to the earth along with his horse. Zherkov and the staff officer ducked over their saddles and yanked their horses aside. The accountant stopped, staring at the fallen Cossack with wide-eyed curiosity. The Cossack was dead, but the horse still thrashed.

Prince Bagration squinted, glanced around, and, seeing what had caused the commotion, turned away with indifference, as if to say, "Is this really worth stopping for?" He reined in his horse with the skill of an expert rider and, bending slightly, freed his saber, which had caught in his cloak. It was an old-fashioned saber, not the kind in common use anymore. Prince Andrew remembered the story of how Suvorov had given his saber to Bagration in Italy, and the memory felt especially right at that moment. They had reached the battery where Prince Andrew had stood earlier surveying the field.
"Whose company?" Prince Bagration asked an artilleryman standing by an ammunition wagon.
He asked, "Whose company?" but what he really meant was, "You're not scared up here, are you?" And the artilleryman understood perfectly.
"Captain Tushin's, your excellency!" shouted a red-haired, freckled gunner in a cheerful voice, standing at attention.
"Right, right," Bagration muttered, as if turning something over in his mind, and rode past the limbers to the farthest cannon.

As he approached, a deafening blast erupted from it, and in the sudden cloud of smoke that enveloped the gun, they could see the crew straining to roll it quickly back into position. A huge, broad-shouldered gunner—Number One—stood with legs wide apart, gripping a sponge-staff, and sprang to the wheel. Number Two, his hands trembling, rammed a charge into the cannon's mouth. Captain Tushin, short and round-shouldered, stumbled over the tail of the gun carriage as he came forward and, not noticing the general, shaded his eyes with his small hand and peered out at the enemy.
"Elevate two lines more and it'll be perfect," he called out in his thin voice, trying to sound bold—a tone that didn't suit his slight frame at all. "Number Two! Fire, Medvedev!"

Bagration called to him, and Tushin, raising three fingers to his cap in a bashful, awkward gesture—less like a military salute than a priest's blessing—approached the general. Although Tushin's guns were supposed to be covering the valley, he had been lobbing incendiary shells at the village of Schon Grabern, which lay directly ahead, where large masses of French troops were advancing.

No one had given Tushin specific orders about where to aim, but after consulting his sergeant major Zakharchenko, whom he deeply respected, he'd decided on his own that setting the village on fire would be useful. "Very good!" said Bagration in response to the officer's report, and began carefully surveying the entire battlefield spread before him. The French had pushed closest on the right. Below the heights where the Kiev regiment was stationed, in the hollow where the stream flowed, came the stirring, rolling crackle of musket fire. And much further to the right, beyond the dragoons, a staff officer pointed out to Bagration a French column that was moving to outflank them. To the left, the horizon was bounded by the nearby woods. Prince Bagration ordered two battalions from the center sent to reinforce the right flank. The staff officer dared to point out that if those battalions left, the guns would be completely unprotected. Bagration turned to the officer and stared at him in silence with his dull eyes. Prince Andrew felt the officer's concern was perfectly justified, and that there really was no good answer to it. But at that moment an adjutant came galloping up with a message from the colonel commanding the troops in the hollow: massive French forces were bearing down on them, and his regiment was falling apart, retreating toward the Kiev grenadiers. Prince Bagration gave a nod of acknowledgment. He rode off to the right at a walk and sent an adjutant to the dragoons with orders to attack the French. But this adjutant returned half an hour later with the news that the dragoon commander had already pulled back behind the ravine—heavy fire had been concentrated on his position and he was losing men for nothing—so he'd pushed some sharpshooters into the woods instead.
"Very good!" said Bagration.

As he rode away from the battery, firing broke out on the left too. Since it was too far for him to reach the left flank in time, Bagration sent Zherkov to tell the general in command there—the same one who had paraded his regiment before Kutuzov at Braunau—to pull back as fast as possible behind the hollow to the rear, since the right flank probably couldn't hold the enemy's assault much longer. As for Tushin and the battalion supporting his battery, they were completely forgotten. Prince Andrew listened closely to Bagration's exchanges with the various officers and the orders he issued, and to his surprise realized that no real orders were being given at all. What Bagration actually did was try to make it appear that everything happening—whether by necessity, by chance, or by the initiative of subordinate commanders—was being done, if not by his direct command, then at least in keeping with his intentions. Prince Andrew noticed, though, that despite the fact that events unfolded independently of Bagration's will, the man's tact made his presence genuinely valuable. Officers who approached him with worried faces became calm; soldiers and officers greeted him warmly, visibly perked up around him, and clearly wanted to show their bravery in front of him.
